payload.matrix_runs:
PUGH CONTROLLED CONVERGENCE over the blessed front {X1, X2}. X3 is not in the runs — it was eliminated at M4 on a measured property and convergence does not resurrect eliminations.

RUN 1 — DATUM: X2 (one-searcher).
X2 is chosen as the datum deliberately, and against my own inclination. Pugh says the datum should be the strongest viable rival; the temptation was to make the built design the datum and score the alternative against it, which would have flattered the incumbent. X2 is also the CONSERVATIVE choice — no dependency, fewer parts — so making it the reference forces the new thing to justify itself.

  criterion                wt   X1 vs datum   note
  C3 one-click install      5      −          X2 needs no dependency at all; X1 needs a package to resolve a per-platform binary
  C4 structured output      4      +          typed records with spans, against delimited text whose shape changes between modes
  C5 one impl per job       5      S          identical once the job boundary is drawn correctly; deletes the hand-rolled searcher either way
  C6 bounded cost           3      +          native timeout and width caps, against caps we must impose entirely ourselves
  C7 selection correctness  5      S          the guidance mechanism is identical in both
  C8 no migration debt      2      S          identical
  C9 own-failure evidence   5      +          probes P1, P2, P3 and today's measurements all point at the split; none points away
  TOTALS: + = 3 (weights 4, 3, 5 = 12) · − = 1 (weight 5) · S = 3
  Weighted net for X1 against the datum: +7.

RUN 2 — DATUM: X1, per the method's iterate-with-the-winner rule.
The purpose of the second run is not to re-derive the first. It is to ask whether a HYBRID beats the winner — whether the losing candidate's advantage can be grafted on. The only real advantage X2 held is C3: no dependency.
  X2-as-fallback (X1, but fall back to version-control grep when the package fails to resolve a binary): scores + on C3 and − on C5, because it keeps two implementations for ONE question — searching the working tree — which is exactly what the corrected C5 forbids. It also fails C9: an untested fallback path is code we never run, and the owner's ruling on that is explicit. REJECTED, and the rejection is what makes C5's rewrite honest rather than convenient: C5 did not simply get weaker, it now cuts in a different place, and here it cuts against a hybrid I would otherwise have liked.
  No other hybrid was found. The two candidates differ in one mechanism, and there is no third position between 'use the packaged searcher' and 'do not'.

RUN 2 RESULT: X1 unchanged, no hybrid survives.

QUALITATIVE DISCUSSION OF THE HIGH SCORERS, as the method requires before selecting — because the arithmetic here is close enough that it should not decide alone. A net of +7 across a nine-criterion set is not a mandate, and C3, the one criterion X1 LOSES, is weight 5. That is recorded plainly: on the single heaviest criterion where the two differ, the winner is the weaker candidate.
payload.winner:
WINNER: X1 — FIT PER JOB. A packaged fast searcher answers the working tree; version-control grep answers the record; rules are selected by declared applicability with unattached rules reported.

THE WHY BEYOND THE ARITHMETIC, which is the part that actually decides, because +7 across nine criteria is not a mandate and X1 loses the heaviest criterion the two differ on.

IT COMES DOWN TO THE SHAPE OF EACH DESIGN'S FAILURE.
  X1's cost is a package that might not resolve a binary on some platform. That failure is LOUD, ONE-TIME, and IMMEDIATE: it happens at install, it happens to everyone on that platform, and it is impossible to mistake for working. Its mitigation is a documented manual install.
  X2's cost is that our own parser must read two different output shapes, where the ref mode packs two identifiers into the field the working-tree mode uses for one. That failure is SILENT, DATA-DEPENDENT, and LATE: it appears when some path contains a colon, or when an edge case shifts the shape, and what it produces is a wrong answer rather than an error.

This project has already paid for the second kind, repeatedly and at cost, and the requirement register is largely a monument to it: a search that returned confident hits for the literal word 'undefined'; a promotion that reported a red suite because its runner mis-read a crash as a failing test named after a directory; a verification run that executed nothing and reported success. R19 exists because a guard blamed the wrong thing when its own parsing was off. Every one of those was a wrong answer wearing a confident face, and every one cost about an hour to find.

So the deciding argument is not that X1 scores higher. It is that WE ARE BAD AT THE FAILURE MODE X2 INTRODUCES AND WE KNOW IT, from measurements taken today. Choosing the design whose failure is loud over the design whose failure is quiet is exactly what C9 was added to make expressible — and C9 is the criterion the owner's correction created, after observing that our own errors had no channel into the decision.

WHAT THIS DECISION COSTS, stated rather than minimised. X2 was better on the owner's standing bar, and that bar is not decoration: one-click install is a real goal, and X1 weakens it by adding a dependency with no fallback. If that package ever fails to ship a working binary for a platform someone uses, this decision is the reason they are stuck, and the only remedy is a manual install. That risk is already logged, and the owner has already accepted the exposure once — but accepting it a second time, with the alternative now proven viable rather than assumed dead, is a different act, and it belongs in the record as one.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE THIS: if the package fails to resolve on any platform the owner actually uses, X2 is the fallback and it is now known to work — --untracked visibility, ignore-rule behaviour and output shape are all probed. The reversal is cheap because the record contains a viable second design rather than a straw man. That is the concrete value of having reopened the M4 gate rather than passing it with a front of one.

WHAT X1 DOES NOT DECIDE, and must not be read as deciding: the guidance selector's vocabulary — state ids, state kinds, or tags — is identical in both candidates and remains open. Probe P5 measured why it is not free: ten ledger nodes carry applicability at all, zero machine-state nodes do, and its content is prose written for a person. That goes to the spike, and the spike should also record what a semantic selector WOULD have chosen for the same states, so the eliminated third candidate leaves a measurement behind rather than only a rejection.

ONE HONEST NOTE ON THE PROCESS, since this is the state that picks a winner: the winner is the design already built in trunk. I argued at the M4 gate that the front's two survivors differ in a way the code cannot settle, and that stands — X2 was genuinely on the front, the hybrid was genuinely considered and genuinely rejected on a criterion that cut against my preference, and the deciding argument is drawn from measurements rather than from what exists. But I cannot claim the incumbent exerted no pull, and a reader should weigh this decision knowing that.
